strengths: Originality and significance: Learning finite-time dynamics directly from instantaneous force labels is a useful contribution. Adapting start-time Mean Flow consistency to coupled position–momentum dynamics removes the need for trajectory targets or teacher-generated trajectories and permits continuously varying timesteps.

Soundness: Equations (7)–(10) provide a coherent consistency identity, and Appendix C explains its sufficiency in the ideal zero-residual setting. The practical implementation using Jacobian–vector products and independently sampled momenta is well motivated for separable Hamiltonians.

Evaluation: Evidence spans classical mechanical systems, a 100-body gravitational system, five organic molecules, and alanine dipeptide. Structural statistics, short NVE trajectories, vibrational spectra, stability measurements, and timestep ablations provide complementary support. Appendix G.10 usefully tests whether conservation filters alone explain the improvements.

Practical usefulness: Table 7 includes the auxiliary potential evaluation in inference timing and reports approximately 12-fold higher throughput for HFM at 9 fs than the authors' MLFF at 0.5 fs on aspirin. This demonstrates a substantial practical acceleration, although accuracy deteriorates with timestep.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The main derivation is accessible, and the appendices document architectures, sampling, optimization, data splits, hardware, and inference filters extensively. The authors candidly discuss non-symplecticity, thermostat sensitivity, and instability. The stated applications and public benchmark datasets raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: A material simulation-duration inconsistency must be corrected. Section 5.2 and Appendix F.5 describe ten simulations of 100 ns each as totaling 1 ms; they actually total 1 microsecond. Figure 22 repeats the millisecond claim. This is a factor-of-1000 discrepancy in evidence supporting long-duration stability. The actual run lengths and corresponding results need clarification.

The broad dynamical-fidelity claims exceed the strongest evidence. Most molecular evaluation concerns equilibrium statistics under thermostats and conservation filters. Figure 14 provides encouraging short-time trajectory agreement, but the spectra shown cover only low frequencies; sampling at 9 fs has a Nyquist limit of approximately 1850 inverse centimeters. Reference resampling and aliasing treatment are not explained, and transition-rate or longer-time correlation measurements are absent. The evidence supports useful approximate dynamics more clearly than generally faithful kinetics.

Robustness within the advertised continuous timestep range remains limited. Table 15 reports MJS values of 0.5380 and 0.2419 at 10 and 11 fs, compared with 0.0051 at 12 fs. Table 11 also records salicylic-acid failures, including all five runs at 7 fs. These failures are honestly disclosed, but there is no reliable timestep-selection criterion, and local prediction error reportedly does not identify the problematic regime.

Comparative evaluation does not establish the advantage over existing learned long-step integrators. FlashMD and TrajCast are discussed but not evaluated directly. ScoreMD addresses a different supervision and sampling problem. Moreover, Table 1 shows appreciably higher structural error at 9 fs, so fixed-timestep throughput comparisons do not establish an accuracy-matched speedup. Training costs also need clearer qualification: Appendix F.3 reports up to 35 hours for HFM versus 16 hours for the MLFF, whereas the main text emphasizes approximately 30% training overhead.

Theoretical and implementation qualifications need sharpening. Appendix C establishes an identity under exact satisfaction along the relevant characteristics, rather than a finite-data guarantee or convergence result for stop-gradient training. The conservation filter also requires a feasible kinetic-energy target, an appropriate quadratic-root choice, and handling of singular inertia tensors; these cases are not specified. Finally, the code-availability footnote says only 'github' without an actionable repository link. These gaps reduce reproducibility, although the extensive implementation appendix is valuable.

strengths: Originality: Adapting start-time Mean Flow consistency to learn deterministic phase-space evolution from instantaneous force labels is a useful methodological contribution. It removes trajectory generation from training and supports continuously conditioned timesteps. The relationship to existing consistency methods is acknowledged appropriately.

Soundness: Equations (7)–(10) provide a coherent consistency identity, and Appendix C supports sufficiency in the idealized zero-residual setting along trajectories. The empirical evidence extends beyond equilibrium histograms: it includes analytical systems, a gravitational 100-body problem, short NVE trajectory comparisons, and integration and composition errors.

Significance: The method demonstrates practically useful acceleration on the tested small systems. Table 7 includes the auxiliary potential evaluation in inference cost and reports approximately 12-fold greater throughput at 9 fs than the authors’ MLFF at 0.5 fs, although accuracy differs.

Evaluation: The extensive appendices materially strengthen the paper. They examine timestep sampling, training progress, thermostats, conservation filters, and failures. In particular, Appendix G.10 shows useful dynamics without energy/angular-momentum filters and tests whether those filters alone rescue large-step Verlet integration.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The main derivation is readable, and architectural details, data splits, optimization settings, and inference algorithms are extensively documented. The limitations discussion candidly acknowledges approximate physical structure and instability. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: A material reporting error undermines the long-duration claim: Section 5.2 and Appendix F.5 describe ten 100 ns simulations as totaling 1 ms, whereas they total 1 μs—a factor of 1,000 difference. Figure 22 repeats the millisecond claim. The actual run lengths must be clarified before the claimed duration of stability can be accepted.

Robustness is substantially narrower than continuous timestep conditioning might suggest. Table 15 reports catastrophic errors at 10 and 11 fs despite good results at 12 fs, without a predictive timestep-selection criterion. Table 11 also shows all five salicylic-acid runs collapsing at 7 fs. Reporting these failures is commendable; their unresolved cause limits practical reliability.

The acceleration comparison is not made at matched accuracy. For example, aspirin distance-distribution error rises from 0.030 for the MLFF baseline to 0.046 at 9 fs. There is no direct comparison with closely related learned integrators such as FlashMD or TrajCast. The approximately 30% training-overhead statement also needs reconciliation with Appendix F.3’s reported training times of up to 35 hours for HFM versus 16 hours for the MLFF, before counting the auxiliary MLFF used by HFM.

Temporal fidelity is less comprehensively established than structural fidelity. The short NVE comparisons are encouraging, but the spectral comparisons primarily cover low frequencies. Sampling every 9 fs has a Nyquist limit of approximately 1,853 cm⁻¹, below common hydrogen-stretch frequencies; the paper should explain aliasing treatment and restrict its spectral claims accordingly. Quantitative transition-rate or relaxation-time comparisons would better support claims about long-time dynamics.

Some implementation details remain consequential for reproducibility. The code footnote provides only 'github' without a usable repository address. Appendix B.3 does not explain root selection or infeasible conservation corrections: at fixed predicted positions, the target kinetic energy may be below the minimum compatible with the target angular momentum. Handling such cases matters particularly near unstable timesteps.

The demonstrated molecular scope remains small, molecule-specific systems and implicit-solvent alanine dipeptide. This establishes a useful proof of concept, but does not yet substantiate broader scalability to chemically diverse datasets, larger molecules, or condensed-phase simulations.

strengths: Originality: Adapting mean-flow consistency to learn deterministic Hamiltonian evolution from instantaneous force labels is a useful contribution. Equations (7)–(10) provide a coherent route to trajectory-free training, and independent momentum sampling makes the approach compatible with existing molecular force datasets.

Soundness: The consistency identity is mathematically well motivated, and Appendix C explains its sufficiency in the idealized zero-residual setting. Experiments support the central feasibility claim across analytic potentials, gravitational dynamics, and molecular systems.

Evaluation: The supplementary analysis is substantial, covering timestep sampling, training convergence, semigroup consistency, thermostats, conservation filters, and simulation failures. Appendix G.10 provides useful evidence that the learned map contributes beyond stabilization by filters alone.

Significance: Avoiding teacher-generated trajectories while supporting variable timesteps could reduce the cost of learning molecular propagators. Table 7 includes the auxiliary energy-model evaluation in inference timings and demonstrates meaningful throughput gains on aspirin.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main derivation is readable, and the appendices give extensive architecture, optimization, sampling, and simulation details. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges approximate physical structure and instability; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness and reporting: The long-duration peptide claim contains a material arithmetic error. Section 5.2 and Appendix F.5 describe ten 100 ns simulations as totaling 1 ms, although they total 1 μs—a factor of 1,000 difference. The actual rollout duration must be established and the associated stability claims corrected.

Dynamical fidelity is less comprehensively established than equilibrium sampling. The molecular spectra are primarily qualitative and cover only low frequencies; at 9 fs, the Nyquist limit is approximately 1,853 cm⁻¹, below important bond-stretching modes. The manuscript should describe spectral sampling and aliasing treatment and quantify errors in accessible spectra or kinetic observables before claiming broadly faithful dynamics.

Large-timestep reliability remains system dependent. Table 11 reports collapse in all five salicylic-acid runs at 7 fs, while Table 15 shows severe alanine-dipeptide errors at 10–11 fs despite recovery at 12 fs. These honestly reported results are valuable, but continuous timestep conditioning does not establish a reliably usable interval. A validation-based timestep-selection procedure would improve practical usability.

The efficiency comparison does not fully establish an accuracy-matched advantage over the strongest alternatives. Most molecular comparisons use a fixed 0.5 fs Verlet baseline, and there is no direct quantitative comparison with closely related trajectory-trained propagators such as FlashMD or TrajCast. Table 1 also shows increasing structural error at larger steps. The approximately 30% training-overhead statement needs clarification against Appendix F.3's reported 35-hour HFM training versus 16-hour MLFF training, plus the auxiliary potential model.

The theoretical guarantee needs a more explicit scope. Appendix C assumes the consistency equation holds along the relevant trajectories with a regular limit at zero timestep; zero empirical loss on isolated configurations does not supply that guarantee. Nor does the argument establish convergence of stop-gradient training or long-rollout error control. These distinctions matter particularly for claims about sparse or biased training data.

Reproducibility has some unresolved gaps despite the detailed appendix. The code-availability footnote contains only 'github', without an identifiable repository. The conservation-filter derivation also omits the quadratic-root selection rule and handling of infeasible kinetic-energy targets. These implementation choices can affect precisely the stability failures being studied.

strengths: Originality: Adapting startpoint-conditioned mean-flow consistency to learn finite-time Hamiltonian evolution from instantaneous force labels is a useful contribution. Independently sampling momenta makes the approach compatible with existing molecular force datasets without generating trajectory targets.

Soundness: Equations (7)–(10) give a coherent consistency identity, and Appendix C supports its sufficiency under exact satisfaction along trajectories and regularity at zero timestep. The empirical evaluation extends beyond structural statistics to short trajectories, spectra, composition consistency, and Lyapunov times.

Significance: The experiments demonstrate useful acceleration across several systems. Table 9 includes the auxiliary energy-model evaluation in inference cost and reports approximately 12-fold higher throughput than the authors’ MLFF at 9 fs. Table 1 makes the accompanying structural-accuracy tradeoff visible.

Evaluation: The extensive ablations investigate timestep sampling, training horizon, temperature, thermostats, conservation filters, and data efficiency. Appendix G.11 provides valuable evidence that filters alone do not enable large-step Velocity Verlet integration.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main derivation is accessible, and the appendices provide algorithms, architecture specifications, data splits, optimization settings, and hardware details. The limitations discussion candidly acknowledges approximate physical structure and timestep-dependent instability. The stated applications and datasets raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Dynamical accuracy is overstated at the largest advertised timestep. Section 5.2 claims correct Chignolin transition rates at 45 fs, but Figure 29 shows substantial discrepancies: the first-state self-transition probability changes from 0.877 to 0.406, and its transition to state two changes from 0.029 to 0.351. Table 21 likewise deteriorates from 8.11e-4 JSD at 25 fs to 5.11e-2 at 45 fs. Transition comparisons also need an explicit common physical lag and uncertainty estimates.

The safe timestep range is not reliably characterized. Table 17 shows severe alanine-dipeptide failures at 10–11 fs despite good results at 9 and 12 fs, while Table 13 reports collapse in every salicylic-acid replica at 7 fs. Reporting these failures is commendable, but there is no validated selection criterion that lets a practitioner identify reliable timesteps without reference simulations.

Efficiency comparisons do not establish speedups at matched accuracy. Most MLFF baselines use 0.5 fs, whereas HFM structural errors increase at larger steps; a timestep-versus-error-versus-runtime comparison would better quantify the usable gain. The approximately 30% training-overhead statement also needs reconciliation with reported complete training times, such as 35 versus 16 hours for small molecules and 40 versus 10 hours for Ac-Ala3-NHMe, including auxiliary-model training where applicable.

The trajectory-matching comparison in Appendix G.14 conflates objective quality with configuration coverage: its trajectories start from only five geometries, whereas HFM uses decorrelated configurations. This supports a practical advantage under the chosen acquisition protocol, but does not isolate the objectives or establish superiority over trajectory methods with broader restart coverage.

Some theoretical and implementation qualifications remain important. Appendix C establishes an exact consistency result, not convergence of stop-gradient training or finite-sample rollout accuracy. The coupled conservation filter also omits root selection and infeasibility handling: at fixed updated positions, the target kinetic energy can be below the minimum required by the target angular momentum. These cases should be specified for reliable reproduction.

strengths: Originality: Adapting startpoint-conditioned mean-flow consistency to learn finite-time Hamiltonian evolution from instantaneous force labels is a useful contribution. Although the underlying consistency machinery builds on prior work, removing trajectory supervision addresses a meaningful limitation of learned integrators.

Soundness: Equations (7)–(10) give a coherent derivation, and Appendix C establishes the idealized zero-residual identity. The experiments provide substantial evidence beyond structural histograms: short NVE trajectories, semigroup consistency, vibrational spectra, empirical Lyapunov times, and metastable transition probabilities.

Significance: The method demonstrates useful large-step simulation across classical systems, small molecules, peptides, and coarse-grained proteins. Table 9 includes the auxiliary energy-model evaluation in inference timings, supporting a practical throughput advantage rather than merely counting fewer integration steps.

Evaluation: Appendix G.11 meaningfully tests the contribution of inference filters. Spectral agreement persists without energy/angular-momentum correction, while adding filters to Velocity Verlet does not enable comparable large timesteps. Appendix G.14 also provides a relevant trajectory-matching comparison.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main derivation is readable, and the appendices provide extensive architecture, sampling, optimizer, dataset-split, hardware, and simulation details. The manuscript openly reports thermostat dependence and timestep-specific failures. The impact statement is proportionate, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness of the strongest dynamics claim: Section 5.2 claims accurate Chignolin transition rates at 45 fs, but Appendix G.15 contradicts this. Figure 29 changes the first state's self-transition probability from 0.877 to 0.406 and its transition to state 2 from 0.029 to 0.351. Table 21 reports JSD increasing from 8.11e-4 at 25 fs to 5.11e-2 at 45 fs. Stability and approximate equilibrium agreement at the largest step should not be presented as preservation of kinetics.

The theoretical guarantee needs narrower wording. Appendix C establishes exact recovery when the differential identity holds along the relevant characteristics with appropriate regularity at zero timestep. It does not establish that minimizing an empirical loss on finitely many configurations ensures that identity throughout rollout space, nor that stop-gradient optimization converges to it. Explicit coverage assumptions and a distinction between exact consistency, optimization, and generalization would improve the claims.

Accuracy and robustness limit the usable timestep range. In Table 1, aspirin's distance-distribution error increases from 0.030 for the MLFF to 0.046 at 9 fs. Table 13 reports collapse in all five salicylic-acid runs at 7 fs, and Table 17 shows severe alanine-dipeptide failures at 10–11 fs despite better results at 12 fs. These honestly reported findings deserve credit, but they leave reliable timestep selection unresolved and qualify claims of arbitrary-timestep utility.

The spectral evidence supports a restricted frequency range. Figures 7 and 20 show spectra only to approximately 1800 cm^-1; sampling every 9 fs has a Nyquist limit of approximately 1850 cm^-1 and cannot directly resolve fast hydrogen-stretch modes. The manuscript should explain downsampling and aliasing treatment and limit its high-fidelity dynamics claim accordingly.

The efficiency and data-efficiency comparisons need tighter controls. Reported total HFM training times exceed the MLFF times substantially in some experiments: 35 versus 16 hours for small molecules and 40 versus 10 hours for Ac-Ala3-NHMe, which is not captured by the approximately 30% training-overhead statement. Appendix G.14 initializes trajectory matching from only five geometries while HFM receives dispersed configurations, so its low-budget advantage also reflects configuration coverage. Accuracy-matched throughput and comparisons against short trajectories from many starting geometries would better isolate the benefit.

strengths: Originality: Adapting startpoint-conditioned Mean Flow consistency to Hamiltonian dynamics yields a useful trajectory-free learning objective. Equations (8)–(10) use instantaneous force labels and sampled momenta, avoiding trajectory generation while supporting continuously variable timesteps.

Soundness: The consistency identity is well motivated, and Appendix C establishes sufficiency in the idealized exact-residual setting. The implementation is concrete, using Jacobian–vector products and a stop-gradient target.

Significance: The empirical results demonstrate useful acceleration across classical mechanics, small molecules, peptides, and coarse-grained proteins. Table 9 includes the auxiliary energy-model evaluation in inference timings and reports 378.5 ns/day for aspirin at 9 fs versus 31.7 ns/day for the authors’ MLFF baseline.

Evaluation: The extensive appendices examine structural distributions, spectra, short trajectories, semigroup consistency, temperature robustness, training dynamics, and filter effects. Appendix G.11 provides valuable evidence that conservation filters alone do not enable large-step Velocity Verlet integration.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main derivation is clear, and the appendices document architectures, sampling, optimization, data splits, hardware, and simulation settings. The limitations discussion candidly acknowledges non-symplecticity, thermostat dependence, and instability. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Dynamical fidelity is overstated at the largest timesteps. Section 5.2 claims correct Chignolin transition rates at 45 fs, but Figure 29 shows substantial discrepancies: the state-1 self-transition probability changes from 0.877 to 0.406, while Table 21’s JSD rises from 8.11e-4 at 25 fs to 5.11e-2 at 45 fs. The supported timestep range for accurate kinetics should be distinguished from that for stable sampling. Explicit transition-estimation lag times and uncertainty estimates would strengthen this evidence.

The spectral validation has a restricted frequency range. Figures 7 and 20 show spectra only up to approximately 1500 cm^-1; sampling every 9 fs has a Nyquist limit near 1850 cm^-1 and cannot directly resolve fast hydrogen-stretch vibrations. The manuscript should explain downsampling and aliasing treatment and qualify its claims of recovering the correct frequency modes.

Efficiency comparisons do not fully establish matched-accuracy gains. Table 1’s aspirin distance-distribution error increases from 0.030 for the MLFF to 0.046 for HFM at 9 fs, and other molecules also degrade. Table 9 fixes MLFF timesteps at 0.5 fs rather than comparing throughput at matched observable error. Moreover, Appendix F.3 reports up to 35 hours of HFM training versus 16 hours for the MLFF, before accounting for the auxiliary model; the approximately 30% training-overhead statement needs clearer separation from total training cost.

The trajectory-matching comparison in Appendix G.14 confounds the objective with configuration coverage: its baseline receives trajectories initialized from only five geometries, whereas HFM receives dispersed configurations. This is a relevant acquisition scenario, but it does not isolate the benefit of the objective or establish superiority over stronger trajectory-distillation pipelines using more diverse starts.

The theoretical guarantee and practical operating range need sharper qualification. Appendix C assumes the consistency equation holds along the relevant trajectories; zero empirical loss on finitely many snapshots does not establish that condition or convergence of stop-gradient training. Experimentally, alanine dipeptide fails severely at 10–11 fs despite working at 12 fs (Table 17), leaving timestep selection without a reliable diagnostic. These issues limit the reach of an otherwise useful and technically credible contribution.
